notes.title: HeavenX Devlog 0003
notes.content:
[p]Independent video games have existed basically since the medium’s creation, though it wasn’t until relatively recently that releasing one’s passion projects to a global audience became feasible. The advent of the online marketplace has changed the way smaller creators can distribute content. Where once a finished product would have been relinquished to Cool Math Games for students to play in their labs during computer applications class, there now exists a glossy Steam page for it, with a great big Add To Cart button beside a piece of shiny capsule art. [/p][p]The genie is out of the bottle. Game development, now more than ever, is for anyone. But it is certainly not for everyone. You need to be ready to put an unthinkable amount of time and effort into the grind, and even then you will need to steel yourself for disappointment. As it turns out, many are brave or stupid enough to take the plunge; and they walk among you… 
[/p][h2][b]The Water Cooler[/b][/h2][p]No one working on HeavenX does game development for a living. We’d guess that we’re not alone. This is the kind of industry that puts bread on the table for only a select few, and getting anywhere requires a few years in the mud to prove your worth. In the meantime, we gather in the break room at your office, earning an honest living and biding our time. [/p][p]Maybe one day we’ll be free from the rat race. Free to pursue our own dreams on our own terms. Free from the well-loved office bathrooms and the droning hum of its fluorescent lights. [/p][p]Maybe not, though. Perhaps we’ll just gracefully age around the water cooler until it’s finally time to retire. If that time ever comes… [/p][p]It was within the absurdity of office life that we found the soul of HeavenX’s narrative. During one of our stand-ups, a member of our dev team was exhausted from a busy week of work, and recounted that his higher-up had told him, “I need you to go ahead and remove the term “off the clock” from your vocabulary.” We laughed. It was like something you’d hear in Office Space. A level of inhumanity mixed with droll absurdity that flipped a switch on the direction of the project. HeavenX needed to be an office simulator. The possibilities were suddenly endless. [/p][p]
[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/f0e5c75efcd34a6634151ad5a3c02ff052010c27.png"][/img][/p][h2][b]Hot Around the Collar[/b][/h2][p]All of the work-related horror stories we’d share became fuel for a growing fire of spiteful creativity. The story of HeavenX had always taken place at a megacorporation, but had relied primarily on leaked “reference documents” to move the plot forward. It wasn’t until around then that we decided to tell the story via emails and direct messages to simulate a true-to-life dystopian salaryman experience. [/p][p]Since then, the reference documents have been repurposed alongside a node-based story system. In practice it’s quite similar to a visual novel, taking place within a few chat programs on a digital desktop interface. You interact with your coworkers in meaningful ways that change the outcome of the story and allow you to discover the mysteries of the game's world in an organic, earned way.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/64a64b83d9538e53bdfcedd68ff69aa91dce0057.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][p]Of course, this has provided us with multiple opportunities to pepper in nods to absurdities we’ve encountered in our own work lives. Office jargon, interdepartmental feuds, employee incentive programs, all can be found greasing the wheels of HeavenX’s main story.[/p][p]If you’ve never set foot in an office, we like to think you’ll never have to once you finish our game. If you do happen to work an office job, then we hope that HeavenX is as therapeutic for you to play as it was for us to create.[/p]

notes.title: HeavenX Devlog 0002
notes.content:
[h1]A HeavenX Developer's thoughts on Modding: [/h1][p]When I was growing up and first got a GameCube, one of the first games I played to death was TimeSplitters.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/2c4d113372bea7fc7f4aaab7ffb0258aa0ccfb5a.jpg"][/img][/p][p]It had a map maker, and my brothers and I would stay up way too late building levels and then immediately playing them. That loop of creating, sharing, and playing hooked me early.[/p][p]Later I sank a ton of time into Unreal Tournament 2003.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/d5525789222602e1f62b9deb7761c90b208fb646.jpg"][/img][/p][p]I didn’t make custom maps or game modes for it, but I loved jumping into other people’s work.
There was this one map that was basically a giant bedroom, and you were action figure sized weaving around the bed frame and bathroom door.
Stuff like that massively extended the game’s life for me and showed how much creativity a community can bring.[/p][p]More recently, in a game I helped make called MyFloppy, I built a UGC system where players could draw items like furniture, posters or just whatever they wanted and use them to decorate their Floppy’s room.
Players could even submit those items to a global store so others could place them in their rooms.
Watching people fill their spaces with community-made art was a reminder of why I like building systems that allow players to contribute to the experiences of others.[/p][p]That through-line is why I wanted HeavenX to be moddable from the beginning.
I want to support the whole spectrum: folks who just want to play, folks who want to tinker locally, and folks who want to tell completely different stories for their own communities.[/p][p]The architectural choices we’ve made: client profiles, a real-time asset pipeline, and eventually an SDK and self-hostable servers, are all in service of that.

[i]-Hunter[/i][/p][hr][/hr][h2]Server + Client Profile System[/h2][p]It’s been powering HeavenX since playtest #2, but we’ve been expanding it to support a real-time content pipeline for the entirety of HeavenX and (eventually) fully offline play and modding.[/p][h3]Why a real-time asset pipeline?[/h3][list][*][p]Fast fixes without a patch. Core game assets are versioned and served from the HeavenX Game Services (HXGS) backend. Clients can pull versions and integrity hashes, then request the exact asset payloads they need.[/p][/*][*][p]We use the same approach for all content types, which keeps the service transport in the HeavenX client compact and consistent.[/p][/*][*][p]Fair leaderboards. Submissions include structured session and loadouts, on the server we normalize timing and compute placements. This lets us audit or cross-check entries, while ensuring that all players submitting scores are using the same set of cards.[/p][/*][*][p]Add content post-launch without pushing builds. Because HeavenX assets are portable (more below), we can provide new content after release and clients fetch only what changed.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/32aec609402f183e4e2a7a0d71319a862733565f.png"][/img][/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h3]Eventual “client profiles” (offline, modding, and self-hosting)[/h3][p]We’re in the process of designing a client profile system where settings control where the HeavenX client loads its data and which features are enabled. Currently we are planning to support:[/p][list][*][p][b]Local (Built-In)[/b]: Uses the assets that ship with the game. No online features.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Local (Modded)[/b]: Loads assets from disk. No online features. We’ll release our HeavenX SDK after launch so you can author custom cards, maps, story content, etc with the same DTOs our tools use.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Server (Official)[/b]: Default profile. Streams official assets from our ZHI server.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Server (Modded)[/b]: Further out: we’ll release the HeavenX server so communities can self-host and stream their own content to anyone who connects.[/p][/*][/list][quote][p][b]Why this is cool:[/b] different players want different experiences... out-of-the-box offline play, local tinkering, or fully custom storylines streamed from a community server... and we want to enable all of those experiences so we are putting in the work to make it happen.[/p][/quote][hr][/hr][h2]On Stop Killing Games[/h2][p]HeavenX's server architecture was intentional from day one.
We’re building for both offline and online, and for both local and server-side modding.
[b]HeavenX will always be playable.[/b][/p][hr][/hr][h3]Where the server stack is today:[/h3][list][*][p][b]Telemetry (SGTA)[/b]: In place. We capture anonymous performance metrics so we can spot spikes, regressions, and platform issues without personally identifying information.[/p][/*][*][p][b]HeavenX Game Services (HXGS)[/b]: In place. HXGS handles HeavenX client auth, assets, users, leaderboards, more. It sits behind a reverse proxy, and the services are orchestrated in Docker Swarm so we can scale replicas under load as needed.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Story system asset support[/b]: In active development (actors, quests, translations, globals). We’re ~80% through the backend work, more on that once the schema stabilizes and we have it all working correctly.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Everything runs behind an NGINX reverse proxy[/b] with the game services isolated appropriately. We ship Postman collections for all APIs, and the stack is portable to other VPS/dedicated hosts because it’s containerized.[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]How this compares to what other games do:[/h2][p]Plenty of games pick one lane: always-online live service, or a purely local moddable sandbox.
[b]We’re deliberately doing both:[/b][/p][list][*][p]Live service layer for quick balance/content updates (no client patches).[/p][/*][*][p]Offline-first profiles so HeavenX remains playable forever.[/p][/*][*][p]Local modding with an SDK using the same DTOs (data transfer objects – you can think of them as assets like "cards") and editor flows we use internally, so creating content won’t feel like a second-class experience.[/p][/*][*][p]Self-hosted servers (post-launch) so communities can run their own canon, cadence, and game rules.[/p][/*][/list][p]This hybrid is harder to build, but it pays off in [b]longevity[/b], [b]fairness[/b], and [b]content velocity[/b].[/p][hr][/hr][h2]The SDK approach (and why modding won’t be second-class):[/h2][list][*][p]Every Unity asset we stream is represented as a DTO (portable data, again think of a 'thing' in the game like a 'card').[/p][/*][*][p]Our internal editor tools are built around those DTOs to author, validate, hash, and publish.[/p][/*][*][p]After launch, we’ll ship an SDK that exposes the same DTOs + pipelines, so the content-creation experience is [b]identical[/b] to ours.[/p][/*][*][p]Because the server code will also be released, you’ll be free to build your own editors if you prefer a different workflow.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/5820907adfdb0d71c26cf15d1118ae31b24efe40.png"][/img][/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]What’s next from here:[/h2][list][*][p]Finish the story system server backend (actors/quests/translations/globals).[/p][/*][*][p]Wire up client profiles in the launcher/settings UI (likely in December/January).[/p][/*][*][p]Author and document the SDK and self-hostable server (code + Docker image) after release. We’ll take the time to clean, document, and support it properly. In the short term we’re 100% focused on shipping HeavenX.[/p][/*][/list][quote][p]If you’re the kind of player that doesn't want to mess with mods and just play through the vanilla experience, tinker, or run your own unofficial campaign that can be streamed to other players, we’re building HeavenX with you in mind.[/p][/quote][hr][/hr][h2]In Other News[/h2][p]Work continues on writing shaders for the office; there's a lot that goes into making a CRT monitor look good.
Just focusing on one aspect—simulating pixels on the screen—is more involved than you might think.
Depending on what angle you look at the monitor, the strength of the pixel effect, the size of the pixels, etc., you can end up with nasty moiré patterns.
Masking out the colors lowers the brightness of the image which needs to be compensated for both in the texture and the shader.
Then the difference between your own monitor's resolution and the in-game monitor introduces problems that would take several more paragraphs to explain.[/p][hr][/hr][h2]UI/UX Throwback: "RightNow"[/h2][p]The in-game "RightNow" application (a corporate-issued task tracking tool the player will use to complete tasks within HeavenX) takes its design inspiration from the aesthetics and UI/UX conventions of late-90s enterprise software.
As part of ZHI's broader design philosophy, every tool within the desktop interface is deliberately period accurate, drawing from the visual and functional cues of vintage productivity suites like Lotus 1-2-3 and Freelance Graphics.[/p][p][b]Hypothetical:[/b] What if you lived 10 years longer but every time you shit it got all over your hands (There is no way to get around it...) would you take this deal?
[i]If you read this part, answer in the comments below.[/i][/p][p]All other applications are being thought through in the same way.
Currently, there are planned (and in some cases already functional) versions of messaging software (Slack / Teams), email, and rudimentary web browsing tools that emulate the design constraints of early corporate software.
Each tool is built to serve functional roles in the player's experience of the game like surfing intranet pages, uncovering hidden lore, parsing internal memos, or chatting with other Neo-Frontiersmen via “Shout!”.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/b8393e69abd04b0f7ae615811d66d0bc181ad346.jpg"][/img][/p][hr][/hr][h3]Thanks for reading[/h3]

notes.title: HeavenX Devlog 0001
notes.content:
[h1]HeavenX Devlog Update[/h1][p]Hello everyone — it’s been a while since we posted any info about HeavenX, so we thought we’d start talking about the progress we are making in a series of devlogs.[/p][p]First of all — [b]huge thanks to everyone who participated in Playtest #3 this past April.[/b][/p][p]HeavenX is a big game with even bigger ambitions. We’ve accepted that doing things right takes time, and we’re in it for the long haul.[/p][hr][/hr][h2]Development Pillars[/h2][p]We have been organizing HeavenX's development around three pillars:[/p][list][*][p][b]Gameplay[/b][/p][/*][*][p][b]Story[/b][/p][/*][*][p][b]Juice/Supporting Systems[/b][/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]Story Systems[/h2][p]The last playtest focused on the card-based loadout and general gameplay feel. We have plenty of ideas to expand both, but we’ve paused major gameplay changes while we tackle something larger: [b]story systems.[/b][/p][p]We've always wanted HeavenX to be story-rich. Over the last six months we finally gave ourselves the runway to build a [b]dynamic, event-driven story system[/b] that talks to the rest of the game.[/p][p]Think reactive moments that unfold over in-game days, across multiple “apps” in, and outside, of your desktop world.[/p][p][b]Example:[/b]
An NPC pings you about a “donut application form.” You print the form (in-game), fill it out, fax it back. Three in-game days later there’s a knock at your office door and a donut sails through the window.[/p][p]That playful, interconnected feeling is the goal we have been shooting for and we aim to share a [b]vertical slice of the story stack[/b] in playtests next year. From dozens of character sheets in Obsidian, to innumerable rough drafts of emails and direct messages in Google Docs, to interactive Twine maps — the game’s narrative has finally found its home in our event-driven story system. Every piece of readable content is being distilled into its final, purest form.[/p][p]
A photograph of the in-game communication system we're cooking up (FPO Art): [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/f24dff8cd4dcaf15627e41ea6e5fb5676efafad7.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][hr][/hr][h2]Engineering Highlights (since Playtest #3)[/h2][p]Behind the scenes, these required significant infrastructure:[/p][list][*][p][b]In-game chat system[/b] (lightweight Slack/Teams-style client) for story delivery and dynamic events.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Node-based authoring tools[/b] to script story content visually.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Logic nodes + variable system[/b] to track conditions and world state.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Editor workflows[/b] to build and test story content at scale.[/p][/*][/list][p]All of this lays the foundation for the kind of narrative we want HeavenX to have. We’re finally close to seeing a working vertical slice that we think you’ll be excited to see.[/p][p][/p][p]An example of what a quest looks like in our bespoke node based quest system:
[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/2cec6edd8d01ef6e778912df581bc99bf56bf234.png"][/img][/p][hr][/hr][h2]Gameplay & Systems Updates[/h2][list][*][p][b]Movement[/b]
Rewritten from scratch. Initially used a third-party library, but now replaced with a custom system that’s more flexible and momentum-based.[/p][/*][*][p][b]3D Office[/b]
Work has begun on replacing the 2D desktop prototype with a [b]full 3D version[/b], including basic interactivity and realistic shaders.[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]Art Progress[/h2][list][*][p]Story system UI and 3D office assets.[/p][/*][*][p]UI assets for the in-game project management software.[/p][/*][*][p]Work in progress for internal communications tools.[/p][/*][*][p]3D assets for the office environment: desktop computer system, filing cabinet, and more to come.

First pass at getting the desktop environment interactable+projected onto a real 3D screen. [/p][/*][/list][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45576950/4ceba444554839ae610f714eed1efa4eeb43f045.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][hr][/hr][h2]Playtest #3 Loadout Card Insights[/h2][p]Analyzed ~1,000 of the longest dives, leaderboard data, anonymous session data, and the game-card catalog.[/p][h3]Core Configuration (frequent picks)[/h3][list][*][p]Standard Controls (basic movement, no downsides/upsides)[/p][/*][*][p]Prismatic Processor (basic pistol weapon)[/p][/*][*][p]Solenoid Core (passive mana regeneration)[/p][/*][*][p]Shifter (basic dash ability)[/p][/*][*][p]Saving Grace (extra hit before desync)[/p][/*][/list][h3]Sleeper Cards (low pick rate, high performance)[/h3][list][*][p]Amplified Receptors (increased mana value multiplier)[/p][/*][*][p]Reretriggerer (re-triggers multiple cards in loadout)[/p][/*][*][p]Divine Emperor (adds suit points but cuts triggers)[/p][/*][*][p]Hyperfix (explode when taking damage)[/p][/*][/list][h3]Data Insights[/h3][list][*][p][b]Grind ≠ Rank[/b] — Dive count and leaderboard placement uncorrelated.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Aggression pays[/b] — More kills strongly correlate with longer survival.[/p][/*][/list][h3]Design Takeaways[/h3][list][*][p]Dial back core configurations or explore alternative handling.[/p][/*][*][p]Keep builds interesting — soft caps/diminishing returns for overpowered combos.[/p][/*][*][p]Improve design of loadout cards based on playtest data.[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]Playtest #3 Feedback Insights (~150 respondents)[/h2][list][*][p][b]Pace & Fun[/b]: ~7.5/10 pace, ~7.3/10 fun. Movement consistently highlighted.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Learning Curve[/b]: Onboarding around cards/mana needs work.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Difficulty[/b]: Starts hard (~8.5/10), but eases (~6.7/10) as players adapt.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Experimentation[/b]: ~7.4/10 — players love tinkering, but card search feels clunky.[/p][/*][/list][h3]What Testers Liked[/h3][list][*][p]Speed and movement feel[/p][/*][*][p]Deck-building & experimentation[/p][/*][*][p]Surreal/retro aesthetic & music[/p][/*][*][p]Short “one more try” runs[/p][/*][/list][h3]Pain Points[/h3][list][*][p][b]Card clarity/UI[/b]: small text, unclear keywords, weak filtering.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Mana system[/b]: hard to read in combat, unclear mechanics.[/p][/*][*][p][b]HUD readability[/b]: health/mana/status get lost in chaos.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Early overwhelm[/b]: pacing + one-hit lethality can feel unfair.[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][h2]Closing[/h2][p]That’s it regarding the playtest. Other team members have been working diligently on their own.[/p][p][b]Thanks for sticking with us. We’re more excited than ever about where HeavenX is headed.

Make sure you Wishlist the game on Steam [/b]for updates straight from Zhaoxing Heavy Industries. Additionally, [b]join our Discord server and social media pages [/b]using the link below for a direct line to our community engagement specialists:

[/p][h3]--> [url="https://steamcommunity.com/linkfilter/?u=https%3A%2F%2Fdiscord.gg%2Fnzd9SgpZ"]DISCORD[/url] <--
